_about.what: Veteran crews (release 2, Brian's pick of 21 November 2026): the crews of a fleet and the pilots and aircrews of an air group learn from every fight, wear a rank for it, and fight a little better for it. Losses made good with men fresh from the schools thin what they know. A corps already keeps its experience (stories.json 'grades' and 'veterans'); with this switch on, every nation's corps, not only the player's, is thinned by its drafts.
_about.switch: g.flags.crews (crews.ts setCrews). Off in the rules, so that history's wars and every hash stay as they were; the interfaces turn it on when a grand campaign is started. With it off nothing here is read and nothing is written.
_about.ranks: The same five as a corps (stories.json 'grades'): Green, Trained, Seasoned, Veteran, Elite, and a chevron for each step above Green.
_about.pivot: The experience at which crews fight at exactly their nation's strength. Crews above it fight better, crews below it worse.
_about.edge: What one whole point of experience above or below the pivot is worth: a fleet's power at sea (its gunnery, its hunting, its raids), an air group's worth in a fight for the sky and over a battle, and its bombers' aim. With an edge of 0.2 green crews (0.1) fight at 95% and elite ones (0.9) at 111%.
_about.gain: What a fight teaches the men who come through it, before the 'left to learn' share (1 minus what they know): 'won' for a fight their side won, 'lost' for one it lost. 'close' is the lesson of flying over a land battle on call. A fleet at sea through a month of war (on patrol, raiding, escorting or hunting) learns the sea's 'month' from the work itself, fight or no fight: the escort groups of the Atlantic became the best in the world without a fleet action.
_about.most: No crew is ever taught past this.
_about.dilute: New ships and new aircraft join with crews trained to their nation's 'train' level for the year; they count for this share of their numbers when what the crews know is averaged, because men are put beside old hands from the first day.
_about.start: What a nation's crews know when the switch first sees them, by the month of the campaign: rows of [turn, sea, air], the last row whose turn has come. Turn 1 is September 1939, 17 is January 1941, 29 January 1942, 41 January 1943, 53 January 1944.
_about.train: How well trained the men are who fill the gaps and man the new ships and aircraft, by the month: rows of [turn, sea, air]. The schools of the nations that ran short of fuel and time fell away, those of the nations with both grew better.
_about.news: A unit of the player's that reaches this rank or higher is named in the month's home news. 3 is Veteran.
_about.weight: How much each ship counts when a fleet's crews are averaged: about the men she carries, so that a destroyer joining a battle fleet thins it less than a battleship does. An aircraft counts as one; a bomber's crew as 'bomber'.

real: Royal Navy: a long-service professional navy in 1939; by 1942 its escorts and cruisers were the most practised at sea, while the wartime entry of 'hostilities only' ratings kept the newcomers' level near trained.

Japan: the navy's pilots of 1941 had 700 hours and more and many had flown over China; losses at Midway and over the Solomons were never made good, and by 1944 new pilots came to the carriers with a fraction of that (the Philippine Sea, June 1944).

Germany: the Luftwaffe's pilots of 1939 included the Condor Legion's veterans; from 1943 the fuel shortage cut the schools' flying hours, and by 1944 new pilots reached the squadrons with half the hours of their American opponents.
United States: a small, well-drilled navy and air arm in 1941, swamped by expansion in 1942; by 1943-44 its schools sent out pilots with more flying hours than any other air force.
Soviet Union: purges and rapid expansion left the air force of 1941 green; the schools and the Guards regiments raised it steadily from 1943.
